newsitem.title: USA: U.S. heat wave not seen affecting hog marketings.
newsitem.headline: U.S. heat wave not seen affecting hog marketings.

text.p: Hog prices rose about $1.50 per cwt since Monday ahead of a heat wave this week, but industry sources said the forecasted 90-degree-plus temperatures should not greatly affect hog marketings, weight gains or overall health.

"I really haven't had reports from producers that hogs were not doing well," said Mike Telford, executive director of the Iowa Pork Producers Association. "You would have to have an extended time of high heat and we have not had that."
Industry sources said this week's heat wave will be too short to greatly affect hog supplies or weight gains.
Telford said cool nights have also eased the stress of the day's hot weather, allowing hogs to continue gaining weight.
"From our standpoint, growth and performance haven't been affected," said Ray Hankes, a Fairbury, Ill., hog producer, of his hogs. "We just shipped a load this morning and they got along real well."

Because producers like Hankes often ship hogs to market during cool morning hours, Midwest hog dealers doubt the heat will greatly affect marketings when temperatures climb into the mid-90s Fahrenheit this week.
A few Illinois dealers said hot weather since last week may have slowed hog weight gains because average weights were down this week.
Iowa Pork Producers' Telford said the lighter hog weights were probably caused by producers selling hogs earlier than normal to take advantage of this summer's high prices.
Cash hogs traded from $60.50 to $62.50 per cwt at Illinois, Indiana and Iowa direct markets Tuesday. A year ago these prices ranged from $56.50 to $59.00 a year ago.
Also, the large tractor-trailer rigs that haul hogs to market feature sprinkling systems that keep the animals cool while in transit.
An Iowa hog dealer said shippers have to be careful not to let hog-filled trailers sit at docks before unloading. Even a short amount of exposure to the midday heat could kill the hogs, he said.
Also, several dealers said 100-degree temperatures would be needed to greatly affect hog marketings and health.
Meteorologists said temperatures could reach to the mid to high 90s F Wednesday and Thursday in some parts of the Midwest, before dropping into the 80s Friday.
